Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning \teaser

One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion
Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning

Yuxin Jiang, Wenqiang Sun, Jiaqi Li, Yuchao Gu, Lvmin Zhang Affiliation: Show Lab, National University of Singapore Affiliation: A*STAR, Singapore Affiliation: Tencent Affiliation: Stanford Universityhttps://showlab.github.io/o2laf    Ivor Tsang, Mike Zheng Shou Affiliation: Show Lab, National University of Singapore Affiliation: A*STAR, Singapore
Abstract

Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O2LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O2LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O2LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

1 Introduction

Videos provide abundant observations of how the world changes, but rarely reveal the actions that cause those changes [3, 66, 8]. This missing supervision limits our ability to learn controllable world models [24, 25, 81, 77, 57, 55, 64, 13] and embodied agents [93, 67, 6, 56, 22] from internet-scale video.

Latent action learning [17, 65, 66] offers a way to recover such supervision directly from visual transitions. A latent action model typically consists of an inverse dynamics model (IDM), which infers a latent action from an observed transition, and a forward dynamics model (FDM), which predicts its consequence:

zt=IDM⁡(xt,xt+1),x^t+1=FDM⁡(xt,zt).z_{t}=\mathrm{IDM}(x_{t},x_{t+1}),\qquad\hat{x}_{t+1}=\mathrm{FDM}(x_{t},z_{t}).

A compact bottleneck limits what ztz_{t} can encode, encouraging it to retain important information to explain visual changes. Learning useful latent actions therefore depends on both dynamics: the IDM must infer the transition, while the FDM must depend on the inferred action to predict its consequence.

Existing methods differ in where pretrained priors enter this pipeline (Fig. 2), leaving a gap on each side. On the inverse side, IDMs are learned from scratch, either on raw pixels [85, 8, 20] or on top of frozen pretrained features [9, 21, 54]. They must learn to infer actions from transitions largely through the FDM’s reconstruction supervision, and such specialized latent action models are outperformed by general visual foundation models [54]. Olaf-World [35] aligns latent actions with an external video representation to improve transferability, but its IDM is still learned from scratch. On the forward side, recent methods adopt a pretrained video generator as the FDM [62, 76], whose initial-frame conditioning supplies appearance, reducing its leakage into the latent actions. However, they keep the standard diffusion recipe, under which the generator can learn to disregard the latent action [76], underusing its prior as a learning signal. Yet modern video Diffusion Transformers (video DiTs) [58] are pretrained at scale to model how visual states evolve over time [82, 59, 41, 71, 70, 7, 50]. Their representations encode rich temporal structure, while their generative dynamics learn to predict complex visual changes. Much of the prior needed for latent action learning therefore already exists inside a pretrained video generator. This raises a simple question: can a pretrained video DiT serve both inverse and forward dynamics for latent action learning? Doing so is nontrivial: the two dynamics place different demands on the same video prior, requiring careful control over what each can access.

We introduce O2LaF, a self-supervised latent-action framework built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize the IDM and FDM from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them independently for their respective roles. For inverse dynamics, we repurpose the video DiT as a feed-forward transition encoder, where action queries extract one compact latent action per visual transition under causal temporal attention. For forward dynamics, we retain the generative role of the video DiT and introduce causal joint prediction, which predicts the future state sequence jointly, conditioned on the inferred latent actions, while preserving temporal causality. Unlike visual synthesis, where training often emphasizes intermediate-noise timesteps [18, 51], the FDM here also provides the learning signal that shapes the latent-action space. At these partially noisy timesteps, the noisy future still reveals much of the target, allowing the FDM to predict the future with little reliance on the latent action. We therefore train at high noise, which suppresses this target leakage and forces the FDM to depend on the inferred action. The two dynamics are optimized end-to-end through a compact continuous latent-action space.

We further systematically study how the two dynamics shape the learned action space. For example, causal joint prediction outperforms autoregressive prediction by removing clean-history shortcuts, while role-specific noise levels reveal distinct information requirements for the two dynamics. Beyond generative video priors, we also extend the repurposing principle to self-supervised predictive representation models [2] and language-supervised video multimodal models [43] as alternative IDM backbones. Interestingly, stronger action probing performance does not necessarily translate into better downstream generative control, highlighting the importance of validating latent actions beyond probing through downstream applications.

We evaluate O2LaF across camera navigation and robotic manipulation. It sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing across both discrete and continuous action spaces, indicating stronger alignment with ground-truth actions. Beyond probing, the learned actions also transfer without target adaptation, enabling zero-shot control across first- and third-person navigation and human-to-robot transfer in manipulation. The causal FDM readily serves as a video world model, while its learned action-conditioned dynamics provide a strong initialization for higher-fidelity two-stage deployment. Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    We introduce O2LaF, a self-supervised latent-action framework that repurposes a pretrained video DiT into end-to-end trained inverse and forward dynamics models.

  • •

    Through a systematic study, we show that latent-action learning depends critically on how the two dynamics are factorized and what information they receive.

  • •

    O2LaF achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing across camera navigation and robotic manipulation, while demonstrating strong zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments and reusable action-conditioned dynamics for world modeling.

2 Related Work

2.1 Latent Action Learning from Videos

Latent action learning turns large-scale action-unlabeled video into a reusable intermediate control representation. The same representation can be consumed by a world model to control future visual evolution [8, 20, 35, 21, 19], or produced by a policy or planner as a surrogate for physical actions [66, 85, 9, 14, 15, 83]. Recent work further seeks to make this control space transferable across contexts and embodiments [35, 31, 4, 37].

Existing methods differ in where pretrained priors enter the inverse–forward dynamics pipeline (Fig. 2). Early approaches learn both transition inference and prediction directly from the target videos [66, 8, 85, 20]. To reduce shortcuts from raw-pixel reconstruction, later methods move the prediction target into pretrained semantic feature spaces, emphasizing motion and task-relevant change over appearance details [15, 9, 74]. A related direction strengthens the forward model with pretrained video priors, reducing appearance burden or replacing the from-scratch FDM [62, 76, 48]. Pretrained video representations have also been used as external temporal supervision to orient latent actions across visual contexts [35].

Orthogonal to where the prior enters, prior work also constrains the latent space through discrete or continuous bottlenecks [21, 48, 10], semantic or cross-view objectives [42, 88, 40, 34], motion and consistency supervision [5, 11, 79, 16], and physical or geometric grounding [14, 80]. These constraints are complementary to the structural question of how the dynamics themselves are initialized. Motivated by the shared need for transition reasoning in both inverse and forward dynamics, O2LaF repurposes the same pretrained video DiT for both.

2.2 Repurposing Pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers

Pretrained video generative models encode reusable spatiotemporal structure beyond synthesis. Prior work exploits their internal representations for correspondence, tracking, and geometry [53, 60, 68], while more recent methods repurpose the generative backbone itself for feed-forward perception and temporal reasoning [75, 89, 52]. Together, these works show that video generative pretraining provides reusable temporal computation, not only a synthesis model.

This repurposing is increasingly extending to action learning. Recent robot-policy and world-action models use pretrained video generators as predictive representations, policy backbones, or priors for action experts [30, 38, 84, 49, 87, 23]. These methods transfer video priors into learning a physical action space grounded by robot supervision. O2LaF instead uses the video prior to discover the action representation itself from action-free video.

3 Method

We introduce O2LaF, a self-supervised latent action learning framework. Our key premise is that large-scale video pretraining already captures how visual states evolve, which both inverse and forward dynamics need. We therefore initialize both from the same pretrained prior, but adapt each to its role by controlling what information it can access.

3.1 Preliminaries and Motivation

Pretrained Video DiT. O2LaF builds on a pretrained text-to-video model [71, 72] consisting of a video VAE, a text encoder, and a video DiT. The VAE maps an RGB video 𝐕\mathbf{V} to K+1K{+}1 spatiotemporal latent states 𝐱=(x0,…,xK)\mathbf{x}=(x_{0},\ldots,x_{K}). Under rectified flow [47, 18], a clean video latent 𝐱\mathbf{x} is interpolated with Gaussian noise ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) as 𝐱t=(1−t)​𝐱+t​ϵ\mathbf{x}_{t}=(1-t)\mathbf{x}+t\boldsymbol{\epsilon}, with target velocity 𝐯⋆=ϵ−𝐱\mathbf{v}^{\star}=\boldsymbol{\epsilon}-\mathbf{x}. Here, t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1], where t=0t=0 corresponds to clean video latents and t=1t=1 to pure Gaussian noise.

Action-aware video prior. Prior work [53, 52, 60, 68] has shown that pretrained video DiTs contain strong temporal correspondence, enabling subjects or points to be tracked across video frames. We ask a different question: do these models also attend to regions relevant to the ongoing action? We conduct a simple diagnostic. We feed clean video latents to a frozen video DiT at t=0t=0 with the text condition “What is the action in the video?” and visualize the resulting cross-attention. As shown in Fig. 3, the responses follow the active hands and manipulated regions, shifting as the interaction changes across frames and clips. Although qualitative, this observation motivates repurposing the pretrained video prior for transition-level action inference.

3.2 Problem Formulation: One Prior, Two Dynamics

Given an action-unlabeled video, our goal is to infer one compact latent action zi∈ℝdzz_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{z}} for each transition xi→xi+1x_{i}\rightarrow x_{i+1}. We couple an IDM qϕq_{\phi}, which infers latent actions from observed video, with an FDM fθf_{\theta}, which predicts their visual consequences:

zi∼qϕ​(zi∣𝐱~≤i+1IDM,tIDM),𝐯^=fθ​(𝐱~FDM,tFDM,𝐜0,𝐳¯).z_{i}\sim q_{\phi}\left(z_{i}\mid\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}}_{\leq i+1},t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}}\right),\qquad\widehat{\mathbf{v}}=f_{\theta}\left(\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}},t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}},\mathbf{c}_{0},\overline{\mathbf{z}}\right). (1)

Here, 𝐜0=“a video”\mathbf{c}_{0}=\text{``a video''} is a fixed neutral text condition, and 𝐳¯=[ 0,z0,…,zK−1]\overline{\mathbf{z}}=[\,0,z_{0},\ldots,z_{K-1}\,] aligns each ziz_{i} with the prediction of xi+1x_{i+1}, and 𝐱~IDM\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{IDM}} and 𝐱~FDM\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{FDM}} denote the respective inputs at independently sampled flow timesteps. Both dynamics are initialized from the same pretrained video DiT [72, 71] and adapted independently with LoRA [29]. The new action-readout and action-conditioning modules are trained from scratch.

3.3 Video DiT as Inverse Dynamics

The IDM repurposes the pretrained video DiT from an iterative generator into a single-pass latent action encoder.

Feed-forward repurposing. Unlike video generation, inverse dynamics operates on an observed video and requires no iterative denoising. We therefore perform a single video DiT forward pass at an IDM flow timestep tIDMt_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}} [75]. The input is constructed as 𝐱~IDM=(1−tIDM)​𝐱+tIDM​ϵ.\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}}=(1-t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}})\mathbf{x}+t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}}\boldsymbol{\epsilon}. At tIDM=0t_{\mathrm{IDM}}=0, the model receives clean video latents, while increasing the timestep progressively removes visual information. This provides a flexible family of noise-dependent representations from which to infer actions.

Transition readout with action queries. To extract transition-level information, we introduce learnable action queries into the video DiT. A shared query embedding is replicated across transitions, with temporal position encoding distinguishing each query qiq_{i} associated with xi→xi+1x_{i}\rightarrow x_{i+1}. We employ an asymmetric attention mask (Fig. 4): (i) video tokens attend causally across frames, (ii) each action query qiq_{i} reads only the two endpoint states (xi,xi+1)(x_{i},x_{i+1}), and (iii) action queries do not attend to one another, nor do video tokens attend to the queries. This makes each query a read-only transition register rather than an auxiliary communication channel.

Variational action bottleneck. Let hi∈ℝDh_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the final representation of action query qiq_{i}. We use a linear Gaussian head gϕ:ℝD→ℝ2​dzg_{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{D}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2d_{z}}, with dz≪Dd_{z}\ll D, to obtain a compact latent action:

[μi,log⁡σi2]=gϕ​(LN⁡(hi)),qϕ​(zi∣𝐱~≤i+1IDM,tIDM)=𝒩⁡(μi,diag⁡(σi2)).[\,\mu_{i},\log\sigma_{i}^{2}\,]=g_{\phi}\!\left(\operatorname{LN}(h_{i})\right),\qquad q_{\phi}\!\left(z_{i}\mid\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathrm{IDM}}_{\leq i+1},t_{\mathrm{IDM}}\right)=\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_{i},\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{i}^{2})\right). (2)

During training, we sample zi=μi+σi⊙ξiz_{i}=\mu_{i}+\sigma_{i}\odot\xi_{i}, where ξi∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\xi_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) and use the posterior mean μi\mu_{i} at inference. The continuous latent space avoids quantization, allowing fine-grained variations in visual dynamics to be represented [20, 21, 35].

3.4 Video DiT as Forward Dynamics

The FDM predicts the visual consequences of inferred latent actions, providing the predictive supervision for the IDM. To make this supervision informative, we adapt the pretrained video DiT’s temporal structure and conditioning to control information access, limiting visual shortcuts while preserving its generative capability.

Initial-state and action conditioning. The FDM receives the clean initial state x0x_{0} and the temporally aligned latent-action sequence 𝐳¯\overline{\mathbf{z}}. The initial state provides visual context, including appearance and spatial structure, outside the latent-action bottleneck [62], encouraging latent actions to capture transferable dynamics rather than scene-specific appearance. Following standard DiT conditioning [58], the aligned actions are projected, combined with the corresponding flow-timestep embeddings, and injected into every Transformer block through AdaLN.

Causal joint flow matching. We keep x0x_{0} clean and add noise to all future states using a shared timestep tFDMt_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}: 𝐱~FDM=[x0,x1tFDM,…,xKtFDM],xitFDM=(1−tFDM)​xi+tFDM​ϵi.\widetilde{\mathbf{x}}^{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}=[\,x_{0},x^{t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}}_{1},\ldots,x^{t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}}_{K}\,],x^{t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}}_{i}=(1-t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}})x_{i}+t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}\epsilon_{i}. The velocities of all future states are predicted jointly in a single forward pass at each flow timestep. To prevent information leakage from later states, we replace the pretrained video DiT’s bidirectional temporal attention with frame-causal attention, such that tokens at xix_{i} cannot attend to later states x>ix_{>i}. When conditioned on clean preceding frames, autoregressive prediction can exploit temporal redundancy by simply copying the previous frame, bypassing the latent-action bottleneck. By removing this clean-history shortcut, causal joint prediction encourages the FDM to leverage latent actions, providing more effective supervision to the IDM.

High-noise timestep sampling. Causal attention prevents future-state leakage, but each prediction still observes its own noisy target. Common generative training recipes emphasize intermediate noise levels. For example, SD3 [18] uses logit-normal timestep sampling, whose density vanishes at both endpoints. While effective for visual generation, this middle-noise bias is undesirable for latent-action learning: noisy future states may still retain sufficient information for the FDM to predict future states without fully utilizing latent actions. We therefore emphasize high-noise tFDMt_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}, reducing information available from the noisy targets and encouraging the FDM to rely more strongly on latent actions. The endpoint tFDM=1t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}=1 makes this intuition explicit. For future state xix_{i}, vi⋆=ϵi−xiv_{i}^{\star}=\epsilon_{i}-x_{i}. Defining x^i=ϵi−v^i\hat{x}_{i}=\epsilon_{i}-\hat{v}_{i} gives ‖v^i−vi⋆‖22=‖x^i−xi‖22.\left\|\hat{v}_{i}-v_{i}^{\star}\right\|_{2}^{2}=\left\|\hat{x}_{i}-x_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}. Thus, at pure noise, flow matching is equivalent to reconstructing the future latent conditioned on the clean initial state and latent actions.

3.5 End-to-End Latent Action Learning

The IDM and FDM are connected through the sampled latent actions and optimized end-to-end (Fig. 5).

Role-specific noise sampling. Noise plays different roles in the two dynamics. For the IDM, it controls the visual information available for transition inference. For the FDM, it controls how much target information remains accessible through the noisy future states. We therefore sample their flow timesteps independently: tIDM∼πIDM,tFDM∼πFDM.t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}}\sim\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}},t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}\sim\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}. The two distributions can thus be chosen for their respective roles rather than inherited from the same generative training recipe. In particular, πIDM=δ0\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}}=\delta_{0} corresponds to a clean-input IDM, while πFDM\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}} can emphasize high-noise states as described in Sec. 3.4.

Learning objective. We optimize the flow-matching prediction loss [47, 18] together with a KL regularizer [39, 26] on the latent-action posterior:

ℒ=𝔼[1K∑i=1Kw(tFDM)‖v^i−(ϵi−xi)‖22]+βK∑i=0K−1DKL[qϕ(zi∣⋅)∥𝒩(0,I)].\begin{split}\mathcal{L}&=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}w(t_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}})\left\|\hat{v}_{i}-(\epsilon_{i}-x_{i})\right\|_{2}^{2}\right]+\frac{\beta}{K}\sum_{i=0}^{K-1}D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left[q_{\phi}(z_{i}\mid\cdot)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(0,I)\right].\end{split} (3)

Through reparameterization, gradients from the FDM propagate through the latent actions into the IDM. The prediction loss guides the IDM to encode transition information essential for explaining future visual changes, while the low-dimensional latent space and KL regularization constrain the information carried by the action channel.

Inference and action transfer. While the FDM shapes the latent-action space during training, it serves as an action-conditioned video world model at inference. Given an initial state and inferred latent actions, we initialize future latents from Gaussian noise and integrate the learned flow from t=1t=1 to t=0t=0 using the Euler solver [18]. Actions inferred from a source video can thus condition generation from a different initial state, enabling zero-shot cross-context action transfer.

4 Experiments

We evaluate O2LaF along two questions. First, do the learned latent actions align with real controls across discrete navigation and continuous manipulation (Sec. 4.2)? Second, can the same actions serve as a unified control interface for video world model in unseen visual contexts, without target-specific adaptation (Sec. 4.3)?

4.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets. We evaluate O2LaF across two domains with distinct visual dynamics. For camera navigation, we train on MiraData [36] and evaluate on MIND [86]. For robot manipulation, we train exclusively on egocentric human demonstrations from EgoDex [28] and directly evaluate on in-lab GR-1 robot demonstrations [19]. MiraData captures global scene and camera motion, whereas EgoDex focuses on fine-grained hand–object interactions. No action annotations are used to train the latent action models.

Baselines. We compare with representative latent-action methods spanning the learning paradigms illustrated in Fig. 2. For navigation, we compare with AdaWorld [20] and Olaf-World [35], all trained on the same MiraData videos. For manipulation, we compare with DreamDojo [19], VideoWorld2 [62], LAPA-DINOv3 [85, 54], and VILLA-X [14] using their released models. Notably, O2LaF uses only EgoDex subset of DreamDojo’s large scale egocentric training data. We evaluate representation quality using frozen encoders under identical probing protocols, and action-conditioned generation through a controlled second-stage world-model comparison.

Implementation details. Both the IDM and FDM of O2LaF are initialized from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B and adapted with rank-128 LoRA. The IDM uses causal video-token attention, while the FDM uses frame-causal attention with joint future prediction. We use a 32-D Gaussian latent action with β=10−4\beta=10^{-4} and keep the video VAE and text encoder frozen. For all main experiments, we use a single domain-agnostic noise configuration: πIDM=δ0,πFDM=0.7​πbase+0.3​πhigh,supp⁡(πhigh)⊆[0.9,1).\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{IDM}}=\delta_{0},\pi_{\scriptscriptstyle\mathrm{FDM}}=0.7\pi_{\mathrm{base}}+0.3\pi_{\mathrm{high}},\operatorname{supp}(\pi_{\mathrm{high}})\subseteq[0.9,1). Here, πbase\pi_{\mathrm{base}} is the standard shifted flow-time distribution, with peak flow-matching weight assigned to high-noise samples. Sec. 5.2 studies the broader IDM–FDM noise design space across action domains. For a fair downstream world-model evaluation, we train a separate bidirectional FDM for each frozen latent-action encoder, using the same pretrained Wan2.2-TI2V-5B checkpoint and identical training and generation protocols, thereby isolating the effect of latent-action representations. Additional details are provided in Appendix A.

4.2 Latent Action Quality

A useful latent action should make the underlying control easy to recover with little labeled supervision. We therefore freeze each latent-action encoder and fit lightweight linear probes [90] across increasing label budgets to evaluate control decodability.

Evaluation protocol. We evaluate discrete camera control and continuous robot manipulation. On MIND, we predict four simultaneous ternary controls (two translation and two rotation axes) using independent, class-balanced logistic regression probes. We report joint exact-match accuracy, requiring all four predictions to be correct. For manipulation, we use DreamDojo’s In-lab Eval benchmark [19], comprising GR-1 robot demonstrations. We fit Ridge regression probes for wrist translation and rotation on both arms. We report EEF R2R^{2}, averaged over translation, rotation, and both arms. Label budgets range from 1 to 50 videos for navigation and 1 to 32 episodes per task for manipulation.

Results. Fig. 6 shows that O2LaF consistently improves linear decodability across domains and label budgets. Performance rises sharply with the first few labeled examples, indicating that control-relevant information is readily accessible with limited supervision. Notably, O2LaF achieves an EEF R2R^{2} of 0.2770.277 on GR-1, compared with 0.1490.149 for DreamDojo, despite training its encoder exclusively on human demonstrations without robot-domain adaptation, suggesting that the learned latent actions capture motion structure transferable across human and robot embodiments. Together, these results demonstrate that O2LaF learns latent actions that admit label-efficient mappings to both discrete navigation controls and continuous robot motions.

4.3 Zero-Shot Cross-Context Action Transfer

Beyond linear decodability, we investigate whether latent actions provide a transferable control interface across visual contexts and embodiments. Given a reference video, we extract its latent-action sequence and condition the FDM on a different target first frame, without any adaptation.

4.3.1 Camera navigation

Evaluation protocol. We extract actions from 24 reference trajectories (12 first-person and 12 third-person) and transfer them to 50 and 20 novel visual contexts, respectively, yielding 840 cross-context generations. All methods share identical references, target contexts, and generation settings. We assess camera-motion fidelity by estimating trajectories from reference and generated videos using ViPE [32], reporting Sim(3)-aligned translation NRMSE and rotation RPE. We separately evaluate visual quality using VBench [33].

Results. Tab. 1 shows that O2LaF achieves the lowest camera-motion errors and highest imaging quality in both perspectives. Interestingly, latent-action CFG consistently improves camera-motion fidelity and imaging quality, resembling the effectiveness of text-based CFG [27]. This contrasts with prior findings that CFG is less effective for predefined action controls [63]. We hypothesize that the learned latent actions form a meaningful continuous motion manifold, enabling CFG to amplify motion-relevant conditioning and improve sample fidelity. Qualitatively, Fig. 7 illustrates the transfer of reference motion across distinct visual contexts. In first-person navigation, O2LaF reproduces the reference camera’s progressive upward reorientation, while baselines exhibit limited motion or inaccurate viewpoint changes. In third-person navigation, O2LaF captures the agent’s rightward turn and leaning posture, together with corresponding background motion, whereas baselines largely fail to reproduce the turn.

4.3.2 Robot manipulation

Evaluation protocol. We evaluate human-to-robot and robot-to-human action transfer using 85 video pairs spanning 20 manipulation tasks. Human videos are drawn from EgoDex, while robot videos come from DreamDojo’s EgoDex Eval benchmark [19], which reproduces EgoDex interactions using the GR-1 robot. Since the task-paired human and robot demonstrations are neither temporally nor spatially aligned, we evaluate direct action transfer qualitatively. For quantitative evaluation, following Garrido et al. [21], we measure self-reconstruction and cross-embodiment cycle consistency (H→R→HH\!\rightarrow\!R\!\rightarrow\!H and R→H→RR\!\rightarrow\!H\!\rightarrow\!R) using PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.

Results. Tab. 2 shows that O2LaF outperforms DreamDojo across all self-reconstruction and cross-cycle metrics, suggesting that the learned actions retain motion information across embodiment. Qualitatively, Fig. 8 illustrates that human reaching motions induce corresponding robot arm movements, while robot actions elicit human reaching and object-directed interactions. Notably, O2LaF preserves arm-specific motion, including the active arm and reaching direction, despite substantial embodiment differences. Compared with DreamDojo, it exhibits more faithful motion correspondence while preserving the target visual context.

5 Understanding the Two Dynamics

Although sharing the same pretrained video prior, the IDM and FDM serve distinct roles in latent action learning. We systematically investigate how their design choices shape the learned action representations and their utility for controllable video generation.

5.1 Adapting Pretrained Dynamics

Pretrained video DiTs encode rich spatiotemporal knowledge, but their representations are not explicitly optimized for action inference. We investigate whether this knowledge can be extracted through a lightweight action head or requires adapting the pretrained backbone. Since the IDM learns through predictive supervision from the FDM, we further study whether a stronger FDM improves the learned action representations.

Tab. 3(a) shows that a frozen video DiT with a trainable action head performs substantially worse than LoRA adaptation, while rank-16 LoRA approaches rank-128 performance. Meanwhile, scaling the FDM from 1.3B to 14B consistently improves action decodability with a fixed-size IDM (Tab. 3(b)). These results suggest that effective latent-action learning benefits from both adapting pretrained representations and strengthening predictive supervision.

5.2 Controlling Information Exposure

We revisit how the information-access designs of our two dynamics shape latent-action learning.

Temporal factorization. We investigate how the FDM’s temporal prediction structure shapes the learned actions. As shown in Tab. 3(c), causal joint prediction substantially outperforms autoregression across both navigation perspectives and achieves the strongest overall probing performance.

Role-specific noise levels. Motivated by the view of diffusion noise as partial masking [12], we investigate how noise exposure in the two dynamics shape latent-action learning. We conduct a 5×55\times 5 sweep over fixed (tIDM,tFDM)(t_{\mathrm{IDM}},t_{\mathrm{FDM}}) pairs across navigation and manipulation. Fig. 9 reveals three findings. First, moderate IDM noise often improves action decodability over clean inputs, potentially favoring higher-level, action-relevant features over appearance-specific details [69]. Second, low FDM noise yields poor representations, consistent with shortcuts through partially observed targets. However, maximal noise is not always optimal, potentially due to high-variance velocity targets near the noise prior [78], which weakens predictive supervision for the IDM. Finally, preferred noise configurations vary across domains: both navigation perspectives favor (tIDM,tFDM)=(0.3,0.98)(t_{\mathrm{IDM}},t_{\mathrm{FDM}})=(0.3,0.98), whereas manipulation exhibits different optima across arms.

5.3 Extending to Other Video Priors

Our inverse-forward dynamics framework extends beyond generative video DiTs to other video representations. We explore four IDM backbones spanning distinct learning paradigms: (i) ST-Transformer [8], a spatiotemporal Transformer trained from scratch, (ii) VideoChat3 [43], a language-aligned video MLLM, (iii) V-JEPA2 [2], a self-supervised predictive video encoder, and (iv) Wan2.2 [72], a generative video DiT. We similarly adapt each backbone as an IDM by introducing causal temporal attention and learnable action queries, while retaining the same FDM design.

Tab. 4 reveals distinct behaviors. Notably, V-JEPA2 achieves the strongest action probing performance, yet its latent actions exhibit noticeable source-appearance leakage during cross-context generation (Fig. 10). Color probing further confirms substantially higher appearance decodability in V-JEPA2 latent actions, whereas Wan2.2 better preserves the target scene. We hypothesize that sharing a generative video prior between the IDM and FDM improves their representation alignment, facilitating more transferable generative control. It highlights that action probing alone does not reveal whether latent actions also encode task-irrelevant information that may hinder transfer. Downstream generative evaluation is therefore essential for assessing the transferability of learned action representations.

5.4 Balancing Action Learning and Generation

Jointly learning latent actions and a generative video world model is a compelling objective [76]. Yet the FDM faces a practical trade-off: learning informative actions requires limiting visual shortcuts, whereas high-fidelity generation benefits from broader noise coverage. In O2LaF, causal prediction and high-noise supervision serve the former objective, but compromise the latter. We investigate whether both objectives can be reconciled within end-to-end training.

We first study FDM noise sampling and IDM gradient routing. Tab. 5 shows that mixed noise sampling substantially improves generation over high-noise-only training while maintaining comparable action probing performance. However, restricting IDM gradients to high-noise timesteps provides no consistent probing gains. Given the inherent tension, we adopt a two-stage approach [35], freezing the learned IDM and training a bidirectional FDM. This substantially improves generation quality. Moreover, initializing from the jointly trained FDM, rather than the original pretrained video DiT, further improves both visual quality and action-following fidelity.

6 Conclusion

We presented O2LaF, a self-supervised framework that repurposes a pretrained video DiT for both inverse and forward dynamics. By tailoring the two dynamics to their distinct roles and controlling information access, O2LaF learns transferable latent actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, it achieves state-of-the-art few-shot action probing and enables zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and human–robot embodiments. These findings establish pretrained video generators as reusable dynamics priors for action discovery and controllable world modeling.

Limitations and future work. Future work includes improving the interpretability of the learned latent-action space and extending video-predictive dynamics to efficient planning and closed-loop control. See Appendix D for further discussion.

Appendix

The document provides supplementary information not elaborated on in our main paper due to space constraints: implementation details (Section A), visualization of action-query attention (Section B.1) and analysis of training data composition (Section B.2), two applications that use the IDM as a motion annotator and the FDM as a policy verifier (Section C), and a discussion of limitations and future directions (Section D).

Appendix A Implementation Details

A.1 End-to-End Latent-Action Learning

Both the IDM and FDM are initialized from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B [72], with frozen video VAE and text encoder. We adapt both video DiTs using rank-128 LoRA, while directly training the IDM action queries and Gaussian readout, and the FDM action embedder. Each visual transition is represented by a 32-dimensional Gaussian latent action. The IDM uses frame-causal attention with pairwise action queries, while the FDM uses frame-causal attention to denoise future frames conditioned on a clean initial frame. Training configurations are summarized in Tab. 6.

A.2 Two-Stage Video World Model

To improve visual generation quality, we freeze the learned IDM as a latent-action extractor and train a separate bidirectional Wan2.2-TI2V-5B world model conditioned on the extracted actions. The FDM is fully fine-tuned at 832×480832\times 480 resolution. By default, the FDM is initialized from the pretrained text/image-to-video model. For the E2E-init setting, we instead initialize it from the jointly trained causal FDM, providing an initialization already aligned with the learned latent-action space.

Appendix B More Analysis

B.1 Visualizing Action-Query Attention

To understand how the IDM extracts latent actions from visual transitions, we visualize the attention from learned action queries to their corresponding source and target frames. For transition xi→xi+1x_{i}\!\rightarrow x_{i+1}, action query qiq_{i} jointly attends to the spatial tokens of both frames. At transformer block ℓ\ell and head hh, we compute

=softmax⁡([qiℓ,h​(Kiℓ,h)⊤,qiℓ,h​(Ki+1ℓ,h)⊤]dh).\displaystyle=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{[q_{i}^{\ell,h}(K_{i}^{\ell,h})^{\top},\,q_{i}^{\ell,h}(K_{i+1}^{\ell,h})^{\top}]}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\right). (4)

The softmax is computed jointly over both frames, preserving their relative attention mass. The attention maps have a spatial resolution of 15×2615\times 26 and are bicubically upsampled to the RGB frames. For each head and video, we normalize attention by the 99th percentile across all transitions and both frames, followed by clipping to [0,1][0,1]. We visualize the resulting maps using the TURBO colormap with gamma correction (γ=0.8\gamma=0.8) and attention-dependent opacity. Source and target frames share the same normalization scale, without frame-wise renormalization or head aggregation.

As shown in Fig. 11, action-query attention often concentrates on moving agents, manipulated objects, and hand or end-effector interaction regions. These attended regions evolve across transitions, suggesting that the learned queries extract spatially localized evidence from visual changes.

B.2 Analyzing Training Data Composition

Although learned without action annotations, latent-action representations still depend on the motion and embodiment diversity of the training videos. We compare four configurations: MiraData [36] (navigation), EgoDex [28] (human manipulation), EgoDexMix (human and robot manipulation), and joint MiraData/EgoDexMix training. EgoDexMix augments human demonstrations with real robot videos from GR-1 [19] and PH2D [61]. All configurations are evaluated on MIND and In-lab GR-1 following Sec. 4.2.

Tab. 7 reveals a trade-off between domain specialization and cross-domain generalization. MiraData-only training achieves the strongest navigation accuracy, whereas EgoDexMix yields the best robot probing. Notably, compared with human-only EgoDex, EgoDexMix also improves third-person navigation accuracy. Joint MiraData/EgoDexMix training largely preserves navigation performance while improving robot probing over MiraData alone. These findings suggest that diversifying training videos across motion domains and embodiments can broaden the transferability of learned latent actions.

Appendix C Applications

C.1 IDM as a Motion Annotator

O2LaF learns latent actions by explaining visual transitions, without explicit motion annotations. Can a self-supervised IDM provide a better foundation for fine-grained motion understanding? We investigate this on CameraBench [46], which evaluates 15 camera-motion categories. We consider two backbone scales: a 270M spatial-temporal Transformer trained from scratch and fully fine-tuned, and a 5B video DiT initialized from Wan2.2 and adapted with rank-128 LoRA (322M trainable parameters). We compare supervised camera-motion recognition with and without latent-action pretraining, using 1,1141{,}114 labeled CameraBench training clips (1.78 hours). We additionally probe frozen IDMs with lightweight MLP heads to assess their motion understanding without backbone adaptation.

As shown in Tab. 8, latent-action pretraining substantially improves supervised motion recognition, yielding gains of 44.9 and 9.2 AP for the spatial-temporal Transformer and pretrained video DiT, respectively. Notably, the latter improvement comes on top of strong video generative pretraining, suggesting that inverse-dynamics learning captures motion information beyond generic video representations. Even without backbone adaptation, frozen IDM features remain highly effective for motion recognition. Together, these results establish self-supervised inverse dynamics as a promising foundation for motion annotation, with potential extensions to dense temporal labeling and feedback for controllable video generation.

C.2 FDM as a Policy Verifier

Frontier AI models are quickly becoming capable robot agents: they write robot policies as code [44] and control a two-armed robot from camera images in simulation [1]. Such agents are increasingly built and tested in simulators, but a simulator only approximates the real scene, and real-robot trials are slow and costly [91], so a behavior that succeeds in simulation may still fail on the robot. Our FDM offers a cheap check across this gap: starting from a real photo, it predicts what a candidate action sequence will do in the real scene, before the robot executes it.

For each scene, Opus 5.5 (high) rebuilds a MuJoCo [73] simulation from the robot’s head-camera photo, using the GR-1 model from robosuite [92]. We then script candidate grasps and run them in physics as a reference. To query the FDM, we render each trajectory with all movable objects removed, so the latent actions the IDM extracts describe the robot’s motion but not the simulated outcome, and roll them out from the real photo. When the two agree (Fig. 12a,b), the FDM reproduces both a successful placement and a failed grasp, while keeping details the rebuild simplifies, such as the real pan. When they disagree (Fig. 12c), the simulator lifts a salt shaker that, in the FDM rollout, stays on the table. The rebuilt scene suggests a cause: the small tapered glass shakers with metal caps become taller plain cylinders, and the glass vase beside them becomes an opaque cylinder, so a grasp that fits the rebuilt shaker may miss the real one. Without executing the trajectory we cannot tell which prediction is right, but such a disagreement flags an action worth checking before it reaches the robot. We see this pre-execution check as a promising direction for future work.

Appendix D Limitations and Future Work

O2LaF learns transferable latent actions from unlabeled videos, but several challenges remain.

Structure and interpretability of latent actions. Although our learned actions transfer across visual contexts and embodiments, their underlying structure remains poorly understood. Beyond quantitative probing, interpreting individual latent actions still largely relies on inspecting their corresponding reference videos. Learning more interpretable, compositional, and appearance-invariant action representations remains an important direction for future work.

Toward decision-making world models. O2LaF learns latent actions that explain visual transitions and control future video generation. However, its dynamics are optimized for visual prediction rather than decision-making. Unlike compact dynamics models that support efficient imagined rollouts and policy optimization [25, 45], video diffusion models incur substantial computational costs and do not directly expose executable actions or task-relevant rewards. Bridging video-derived action representations with efficient, decision-relevant dynamics is an important direction toward planning and closed-loop control.
